blocks.text: The Hebrews also play their part here, and on this word R. Selomo says: היא קל״בא שו״ריץ ודומה לעכבר הפורח בלילה, "in French it is called calve-souris (chauve-souris, that is, bat), which resembles a mouse and flies by night." Yet [III, 36] Kimchi in his Lexicon writes: כתב רש״י ז״ל כי הוא הנקרא צ״ואיטא, "R. Selomo Jarchi of blessed memory wrote that it is the animal which in French is called chovette, that is, the little [col. 290] owl." However that may be, the most learned of the Hebrews, Baal Hatturim, Aben Ezra, Kimchi etc., hold that it is a bird so called because כל רואה אותה ישום, whoever sees it wonders and is astonished. This must be properly understood. For to wonder or to be astonished is שמם, and the form of the noun does not allow תנשמת thinsemeth to be derived from it, since it plainly belongs to נשם nasam. But in that language it can happen that the same word has two origins, one with respect to its form, the other with respect to its meaning. And you will find not a few words which take their form from the defective Pe-Nun verbs, such as נשם nasam, but their meaning from the verbs doubling the second radical, such as שמם samam. Thus נחילות nechiloth, a kind of pipe, Ps. V, 1., has its form from the verb נחל nachal, to possess, but its meaning from the verb חלל chalal, to pierce, whence also חליל chalil is a pipe, Es. V, 12., and חללים chalalim, that is, pipes, Ierem. XLVIII, 36. And the word נכסים necasim, that is, riches, is by the same reasoning derived from כסס casas, that is, to count. And נארים nearim, that is, the accursed, Ps. LXXXIX, 10., though as if from נאר, has its meaning from ארר arar, that is, to curse. And in Es. XXII, 7. the words המסכה הנסוכה, the veil drawn over, and in Es. XXX, 1. ולנסוך מסכה, and to draw a veil over, although derived from the verb נסך nasach, which is to pour, nevertheless borrow their meaning from the verb סכך sachach, which is to cover and to draw over. And in Lev. XXIV, 11. 16. you will find נקב nakab, i.e. to pierce, used three times for קבב kabab, i.e. to curse. But, not to seek examples further afield: like תנשמת thinsemeth, so also נשמה nesama, properly the rational soul, comes in respect of form from the root נשם nasam, but in respect of meaning they would derive it from the word שמים samajim, which means the heavens; because
Fiery is its vigour, and heavenly its origin.

Kimchi in his Lexicon: לא מצאנו נשמה חוץ מנשמת האדם ורבים אמרו שנקראת כן בעבור שהיא מן השמים ואם הם שנים שרשים נמצאו כמוהו רבים, "We do not find the word nesama except of the human soul, which many assert is so called because it comes from the heavens; and, though there be two roots, many words of this kind are found." From these examples, then, it is clear that the word תנשמת thinsemeth too can be traced back to the verb שמם samam (which means to wonder and to be struck with astonishment), as we have shown is affirmed by the most learned of the Hebrews. Granting this, it will be highly probable that תנשמת is the little owl, at whose unusual form the other birds are astonished. Timon the writer of Silloi, in Laërtius and Hesychius Illustris, on Arcesilaus:
Οἱ δέ μιν ἤυτε γλαῦκα πέριξ σπίζαι τερατεῦντο, [Hoi de min ēute glauka perix spizai terateunto,]
